phonemes.desc: Closed front [i] carrying the stress, which in Quechua falls, as always, on the penultimate syllable.
Unaspirated alveolar [t] plus close [i]; the vowels are pure and even, without the diphthong English speakers often add.

pronunciation.approximation: 'IN-tee' — two even syllables with the weight on the first; the vowels are pure, the t light and unaspirated.

kin.label: Quechua
kin.form: inti, 'sun' — the ordinary noun raised to the highest theonym of the empire; the Cuzco dialect is the source of every chronicle's form (Mannheim, The Language of the Inka)

kin.label: Aymara
kin.form: inti, 'sun' — the same solar word across the two great imperial languages of the Andes

kin.label: Colonial Spanish
kin.form: el Sol / el Sol Inca — the chroniclers' gloss; Betanzos, Suma y Narración de los Incas (1557)

pronunciation.note: Inti is Tier 2: the Quechua name carries no diacritic and no distinctive letter, and the capital alone distinguishes the restoration from the ASCII form. What the temple restores is not a sound but a sovereignty — Inti, the Sun, father and ancestor of the Sapa Inca.

domains.title: Inti
domains.subtitle: Sun
domains.lead: Inti is the sun as sovereign: father of the Inca dynasty, patron of Cuzco, and the divine ancestor whose rays fed the terraces that fed an empire. He is the unseen emperor of the Andean sky — never shown as a body, only as gold, light, and the crimson fringe on his son's forehead.

cards.name: The Punchao
cards.desc: The life-sized golden statue of Inti — 'Daytime' — enthroned in the Coricancha, its face and rays of beaten gold, flanked by golden maize and llamas (Cobo, Historia 13.14).

cards.name: Ancestor of the Sapa Inca
cards.desc: Every reigning Inca was the Sun's son; the empire's genealogy, law, and war were obligations owed to a father in the sky.

cards.name: Inti Raymi
cards.desc: The June festival at Cuzco — fasting, night dancing, and offerings on the usnu, when the Sapa Inca drank with his father at the standing sun (Cobo 13.16–17).

cards.name: Solar Agriculture
cards.desc: Terraces, planting calendars, and frost-shrines along the equator — the sun made harvest, and harvest made the empire.

symbols.name: The Punchao idol
symbols.meaning: The great golden statue of Inti kept in the Coricancha: a round face with rays and a ceremonial fringe, tended each morning like a waking king (Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo 13.14).

symbols.name: The Maskaypacha
symbols.meaning: The crimson tassel-fringe worn on the Sapa Inca's forehead, read as the sun's own rays — kingship made visible as light.

symbols.name: Golden maize and llamas
symbols.meaning: Life-sized gold offerings in the Coricancha's garden of the Sun: the staple crop and beast of burden presented to Inti in his own metal.

symbols.name: The gilded eastern wall
symbols.meaning: The sanctuary's eastern wall was a sheet of gold, catching the first light of the June solstice and setting the whole house of the Sun ablaze.

symbols.name: The June solstice
symbols.meaning: The pivot of Inti Raymi: the sun stands still, the emperor stands before it, and the year is renewed by being witnessed.

mythology.lead: Inti's mythology is imperial theology. The sixteenth-century chroniclers — Betanzos, Sarmiento de Gamboa, Murúa, and later Cobo — preserve the state myths that made a mountain people the children of the sun: a creator who sired the daystar, a brother and sister sent to found Cuzco, and a solstice festival that renewed the world each year.

myths.title: Inti, Child of the Creator
myths.text: In the theology the Inca taught at Cuzco, Inti was not the first power. The creator Viracocha — the incomprehensible god behind the world, as the chroniclers struggled to render him — made the sun, the moon, and the stars and set them in heaven as lights for humankind. Inti and his sister-wife Mama Quilla were thus the children of the highest god, commissioned to govern the sky in their father's place (Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia Indica 7; Betanzos, Suma y Narración 2). The genealogy is political architecture: by making Inti a son rather than a source, the Inca placed their own emperor — Inti's son — only two steps below creation itself. When the Sapa Inca stood before the people as the unique son of the Sun, the title carried a whole cosmology in four words. The myth means that empire, in the Andes, was a family business conducted in the language of the sky.

myths.title: The Golden Staff of Manco Cápac
myths.text: The founding myth of Cuzco is a solar errand. Inti and Mama Quilla, grieving that humankind lived without law, cloth, or maize, sent their children — a son, Manco Cápac, and a daughter, Mama Ocllo — from the Island of the Sun in Lake Titicaca, bearing a golden staff. Wherever the staff sank whole into the earth, there they were to raise the city. At the hill called Huanacauri, above the valley of Cuzco, the staff went down, and the siblings taught the gathered people to plough, to weave, and to live under rule (Sarmiento, Historia Indica 11–12; Betanzos 4; Murúa, Historia general del Piru). The myth makes the Inca capital literally planted in the ground by the sun's own metal: Cuzco was not built so much as sown. Every furrow of its terraces repeated the lesson — agriculture, the technology that let the mountains feed an empire, arrived as a gift from Inti's household, and the ruler in Cuzco ruled as the sun's eldest child.

myths.title: The Vision at Susurpuquio
myths.text: Before he was Pachacuti — 'He Who Shakes the Earth' — the prince Yupanqui was an unlikely heir, and the Chanka confederation stood ready to erase Cuzco. In the account Sarmiento de Gamboa drew from Inca informants (Historia Indica 35–38), the young man took refuge at the spring of Susurpuquio, and there the Creator Viracocha came to him in a dream, and Inti promised that the sun himself would fight beside him. The Chanka attack failed; Yupanqui became the ninth Sapa Inca; and he answered the vision on an imperial scale. He rebuilt Cuzco as the navel of the world, re-founded the Coricancha — the Golden Enclosure — as his father Inti's house, and lined its courts with chambers of gold. The myth's logic is reciprocal and exact: a god gave a man a victory at a spring, and the man gave the god a temple of gold. Conquest and devotion were the same transaction, and the empire expanded, as its own theology said, because the sun willed it.

myths.title: Inti Raymi at the Standing Sun
myths.text: At the June solstice the sun stands still, and Cuzco held its breath. Bernabé Cobo, working from lost eyewitness sources, describes the Inti Raymi, the Festival of the Sun: a general fast; then the Sapa Inca, robed and wearing the Maskaypacha, processing to the great usnu platform of the main plaza, where the mummified dead emperors were set in order to drink with their father (Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo 13.16–17). Chicha flowed, llamas were sacrificed, and dancers circled the night fire in the hides of pumas and condors, every hearth in the city rekindled from the sacred flame. The theology is in the geometry: the emperor faced the sun at the moment it turned, so that the whole state — dead rulers, living Inca, common households — formed a single circuit of light and obligation. The year did not merely pass; it was renewed by being witnessed, and the witness was Inti.

myths.title: The Punchao Carried Away
myths.text: The heart of Inti's cult was the Punchao — 'Daytime' — a life-sized statue of the sun in solid gold, with a face, rays, and a fringe, kept in the Coricancha and tended each morning like a waking king (Cobo 13.14). Pizarro's men stripped the temple's gold from its walls in 1533 and carried the Punchao down to Lima; Murúa records that in 1559 the Spanish even exhumed the mummified bodies of dead emperors from their own shrines and shipped them to the viceregal capital, where the last witnesses lost track of them. Nothing survives of the statue but descriptions — the most eloquent archaeology in the Americas is an absence. The chroniclers' inventories mean that the empire's golden age is known exactly and lost exactly: Inti's temple is a cavity at the center of Cuzco, and the name restored here is the one thing the conquest could not melt down.

lore.syncretism: The conquest did not end Inti; it translated him. Spanish missionaries deliberately identified the sun with the Christian God, and the great church of Santo Domingo was planted directly on the Coricancha's foundations, its colonial vaults rising around the curved Inca walls that still hold them up. Extirpation campaigns under the viceroyalty hunted the surviving cult, and the last great idols of the old religion were destroyed in the 1570s. Yet the translation ran both ways: in the Andean highlands the sun kept his ancient festival day, and in 1944 the Cusco teacher Faustino Espinoza Navarro staged the first modern Inti Raymi at Sacsayhuamán — a theatrical revival, partly invented, that has grown into one of South America's great public rituals, drawing hundreds of thousands each June. The Inca sun survives less as doctrine than as performance: a name the conquest could not melt, re-lit every solstice above the city he founded.
lore.culturalLegacy: Inti's name still circulates as money and memory. Peru's currency from 1985 to 1991 was the inti, and the sol that replaced it remembers the same sun. Cusco's civic emblems carry solar imagery, and the restored Inti Raymi has made the June solstice the city's defining modern feast, performed now in Quechua before an audience of the world. Across Bolivia and Ecuador the sun appears in indigenous political symbolism, and the vocabulary of Inca statehood — Sapa Inca, Coricancha, the sun's own child — remains the standard language of Andean identity. For scholarship, Inti is the paradigm case of religion as statecraft: a god engineered, with extraordinary sophistication, to make empire feel like family.
lore.extendedMeditation: Most sun gods are clocks or lamps. Inti is something rarer: a sun who is also a father, a title, and a border. To be his child was to hold an office; to hold the office was to be luminous by definition; and the whole astonishing apparatus of Inca civilization — the terraces, the storehouses, the road that runs along the equator — can be read as a household administered by the sun's eldest son. The theology solved the oldest problem of government: legitimacy. If the emperor is the sun's son, rebellion is not politics but eclipse, a darkness no subject can afford. Yet there is tenderness in it too: the Inca greeted his father each morning, feasted him at each solstice, and carried his image into battle as a banner of gold. The name restored here is the shortest genealogy in the Americas: Inti — the sun who adopted a nation.

lore.archaeology: The Coricancha — the Golden Enclosure — survives as foundations: the curved wall with the Twelve-Angled Stone (Hatunrumiyoc street) and the trapezoidal doorways and niches now enclosed by Santo Domingo. Nothing of the gold survives; the chroniclers' inventories (Cobo, Murúa) are its only catalogue. Platform-shrines called usnu at Vilcashuamán and Huánuco Pampa mark the provincial stages of the solar cult. The Island of the Sun in Lake Titicaca preserves Inca shrines at the myth's supposed source, including the sacred rock from which the founding siblings were sent. And at Sacsayhuamán above Cuzco the June sun still rises over the terrace where the modern Inti Raymi is performed — here the archaeology is partly a calendar.
